facts.statement: The genus name honors Giancarlo Ligabue, and the species name honors geologist Dr. Héctor A. Leanza, who discovered the skeleton.
facts.quote: The generic name, Ligabuesaurus, honors Giancarlo Ligabue, while the specific name, leanzai, honors the geologist Dr. Héctor A. Leanza, who discovered the skeleton in the Lohan Cura Formation.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen was found during a 1997 expedition at Cerro de los Leones, located 10 km west of Picún Leufú.
facts.quote: One of these expeditions, in 1997, examined a site called Cerro de los Leones, which is 10 km to the West of Picún Leufú.

facts.statement: The species Ligabuesaurus leanzai was named in 2006 by José Bonaparte, Bernardo González Riga, and Sebastián Apesteguía.
facts.quote: These additional remains, which included the specimen MCF-PHV-233, would eventually be described and named in 2006 by José Bonaparte, Bernardo González Riga, and Sebastián Apesteguía.

facts.statement: A second skeleton, specimen MCF-PHV-228, was referred to the genus in 2022.
facts.quote: In 2022, a second skeleton was referred, specimen MCF-PHV-228.

facts.statement: The holotype femur measures 166 cm in length, while the humerus is 149 cm long.
facts.quote: The femur of the holotype is 166 cm long and the humerus is slightly shorter at 149 cm.

facts.statement: Gregory S. Paul estimated the animal reached a length of 18 meters and a mass of 20 tons.
facts.quote: Gregory S. Paul suggested a full size of 18 m long and 20 tons.

facts.statement: The holotype consists of a partial upper jaw with ten teeth, six neck and back vertebrae, shoulder blades, arm bones, and most of the right hindlimb.
facts.quote: The holotype of Ligabuesaurus, MCF-PHV-233, consists of a partial maxillary bone with ten associated teeth, six cervical and dorsal vertebrae, parts of a few ribs, both scapulae, the left humerus, parts of the right humerus, four left metacarpals, and most of the right hindlimb including an incomplete femur, tibia, fibula, astragalus, five metatarsals, and several associated pedal phalanges.

facts.statement: Researchers distinguished the species from other sauropods using unique features of its vertebrae, such as narrow neural spines and unique laminae on the neck bones.
facts.quote: From these remains, Bonaparte and colleagues were able to differentiate Ligabuesaurus from all other sauropods based on several characteristics of the vertebrae including the presence of anteroposteriorly narrow neural spines, relatively short pedicels on the neural arches, and the presence of unique laminae on the posterior cervical vertebrae.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest that multiple fragmentary specimens found at the site likely belong to a single individual due to a lack of repeated bone elements.
facts.quote: Although these elements were found relatively far apart from one another, the lack of repeated elements led Bellardini and colleagues to suggest that all specimens were from a single individual.

facts.statement: The animal lived in the Early Cretaceous period in what is now Argentina.
facts.quote: Ligabuesaurus is a genus of somphospondylan sauropod from the Early Cretaceous Lohan Cura Formation of what is now Argentina.

facts.statement: It lived approximately 112 to 109 million years ago during the Aptian and Albian stages of the Early Cretaceous.
facts.quote: que vivió a mediados del período Cretácico, hace aproximadamente 112 y 109 millones de años, en el Aptiense y el Albiense, en lo que hoy es Sudamérica.

facts.statement: The fossil record dates the animal to between 113.2 and 110.1 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Albian to Albian (113.2 to 110.1 million years ago)

facts.statement: The habitat shared with other sauropods like Limaysaurus, Comahuesaurus, and Agustinia.
facts.quote: Remains from other sauropods are also common including the rebbachisaurids Limaysaurus and Comahuesaurus, and the enigmatic genus Agustinia.

facts.statement: Later analyses classified the genus as a non-titanosaur member of the group Somphospondyli.
facts.quote: Subsequent analyses have recovered Ligabuesaurus as a non-titanosaur member of Somphospondyli.

facts.statement: Some analyses suggest it is a true titanosaur because it is a close relative of Andesaurus, while others classify it as a non-titanosaur somphospondylian.
facts.quote: Philip Mannion and colleagues conducted a comprehensive analysis of all known members of Titanosauriformes. This analysis recovered Ligabuesaurus as being a close relative of Andesaurus, which, per the definition of Titanosauria (the least-inclusive clade containing both Andesaurus and Saltasaurus), would make Ligabuesaurus and its close relatives true titanosaurs.

facts.statement: Its relatively long front legs, with a humerus-to-femur ratio of 0.9, indicate that this trait is not exclusive to Brachiosaurids.
facts.quote: El desarrollo de sus patas delanteras relativamente largas, con un cociente del húmero/fémur de 0.9, indica que esta condición no es una adaptación exclusiva del Brachiosauridae.

rejected.statement: The genus Ligabuesaurus was first described in 2006 based on a partial skeleton that included a skull.
rejected.quote: The type species, Ligabuesaurus leanzai, was described in 2006, based on a partial skeleton with a skull.
rejected.reason: statement copies the source wording: 'described in 2006 based on a partial skeleton'

rejected.statement: A 2022 study estimated the animal's mass between 17 and 29 tons based on bone circumference.
rejected.quote: Flavio Bellardini and colleagues estimated its mass as being between 17 and 29 tons based on the circumference of the femur and humerus.

rejected.statement: The environment was likely heavily irrigated by rivers, as indicated by the siltstone and sandstone composition of the formation.
rejected.quote: The Lohan Cura Formation, where all remains of Ligabuesaurus were found, is composed mainly of siltstones and sandstones, which means the environment was likely heavily irrigated by rivers.
